Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Crabs compete with sea otters for eelgrass as a food source.
Eelgrass beds recover fastest in estuaries without predators.
Sea slugs are the most important grazers in California estuaries.
By reducing crab numbers, sea otters indirectly helped eelgrass beds thrive in an estuary.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Matn otterlar qisqichbaqalarni kamaytirib, bilvosita dengiz o'tlarining sog'lomlashishiga yordam berganini ko'rsatadi. Qolgan variantlar matnda aytilmagan yoki unga zid.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: Paleontologists have traditionally reconstructed the colors of dinosaurs by guesswork, borrowing patterns from modern reptiles. In 2010, however, researchers examining fossilized feathers under powerful microscopes identified melanosomes—tiny structures that contain pigment. Because melanosomes of different shapes produce different colors, the team could infer that one small feathered dinosaur, Anchiornis, had a reddish crest and black-and-white wings.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Anchiornis was the most colorful dinosaur that ever lived.
Paleontologists no longer study fossilized feathers.
Modern reptiles have the same color patterns as most feathered dinosaurs.
The discovery of preserved pigment structures allowed scientists to infer the actual colors of some dinosaurs.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Asosiy g'oya: melanosomalarning topilishi dinozavrlarning haqiqiy rangini aniqlash imkonini berdi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: Aziza Karimova teaches chemistry at a high school in Samarkand. She noticed that many students lost interest when lessons consisted only of formulas on the board. So Karimova began starting each unit with a question from everyday life, such as why bread rises or why metal rusts. Her students now spend the first part of each unit investigating these questions before learning the related formulas, and attendance in her class has risen noticeably.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Karimova's school required teachers to change their methods.
Karimova's students prefer biology to chemistry.
Karimova increased student interest by connecting chemistry lessons to everyday questions.
Karimova stopped teaching formulas in her chemistry class.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Karimova darslarni kundalik hayotdagi savollar bilan boshlab, o'quvchilarning qiziqishini oshirgan.

Central Ideas and Details.passage:
The following text is adapted from Joseph Conrad's 1902 novella Youth. The narrator, Marlow, recalls his first voyage as a young officer.
I remember my youth and the feeling that will never come back any more—the feeling that I could last for ever, outlast the sea, the earth, and all men; the deceitful feeling that lures us on to joys, to perils, to love, to vain effort—to death; the triumphant conviction of strength, the heat of life in the handful of dust.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best describes Marlow's view of his youthful feeling as presented in the text?
choices: He regrets that his youthful confidence prevented him from falling in love.
He considers it a sensible judgment of his own physical abilities.
He recalls it with admiration for its intensity while recognizing that it was an illusion.
He believes he can still recapture that feeling by returning to sea.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Marlow yoshlik tuyg'usini "triumphant" deb ta'riflaydi, ammo uni "deceitful" (aldamchi) deb ham ataydi. Demak, u uni qadrlaydi, lekin illuziya ekanini tan oladi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: Octopuses are often described as solitary animals that avoid one another except to mate. Marine ecologist David Scheel's observations at a site off the coast of Australia challenge that description. Scheel found dozens of octopuses living close together in dens built from discarded shells, frequently interacting through color changes, postures, and occasional evictions. Scheel cautions that the site offers unusually abundant food and limited shelter, conditions that may push octopuses together, but he argues that the behavior shows octopuses are capable of more complex social interaction than previously assumed.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Octopuses everywhere prefer to live in large, crowded groups.
Scheel proved that octopuses build dens only from discarded shells.
Octopuses become aggressive whenever food becomes abundant.
Observations at one unusual site suggest octopuses can be more socially complex than their solitary reputation implies.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Kuzatuvlar sakkizoyoqlar o'ylangandan ko'ra ijtimoiyroq bo'lishi mumkinligini ko'rsatadi, ammo Scheel joyning o'ziga xos sharoitlarini ham eslatadi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: The ancient city of Petra, in present-day Jordan, was carved directly into rose-colored sandstone cliffs more than two thousand years ago. Although the region receives very little rain, Petra's builders designed a system of channels, dams, and underground cisterns that captured water from rare storms. This system allowed the city to support a large population and to become an important stop for traders crossing the desert.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: According to the text, what allowed Petra to support a large population?
choices: A large river that flowed through the city.
Wells dug by traders crossing the desert.
A system that collected and stored water from occasional storms.
Frequent rainfall in the region around the city.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Petrani quruvchilar kamdan-kam bo'ladigan bo'ronlardan suv yig'adigan tizim qurgan, bu esa ko'p aholini boqish imkonini bergan.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: Architect Diébédo Francis Kéré designed a primary school in his home village of Gando, Burkina Faso, using clay bricks made by local residents. Clay was cheap and abundant, and it kept classrooms cooler than the concrete used in many government buildings. Kéré also added a large, raised metal roof that allowed hot air to escape. Because villagers helped build the school, many learned construction skills they later used on other projects in the region.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: According to the text, why did Kéré use clay bricks for the school?
choices: Clay allowed hot air to escape more easily than a metal roof.
Government regulations required clay for schools in rural areas.
Villagers refused to work with concrete.
Clay was inexpensive, widely available, and helped keep the classrooms cool.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Matnda loy arzon, keng tarqalgan va sinfxonalarni salqin saqlagani aytilgan. Issiq havoni metall tom chiqargan, loy emas.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: Some nutrition researchers have claimed that people in certain regions live longer primarily because of a specific food, such as olive oil or seaweed. Epidemiologist Kwame Asante is skeptical of such explanations. In his analysis of long-lived communities in Japan, Italy, and Costa Rica, Asante found that residents' diets differed considerably, but the communities shared other traits: strong social ties, regular physical activity built into daily routines, and a sense of purpose among older adults. Asante argues that focusing on any single food distracts from these broader patterns.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Asante argues that longevity in certain communities is better explained by shared lifestyle patterns than by any particular food.
Asante recommends that older adults move to Japan, Italy, or Costa Rica.
Asante found that olive oil and seaweed have no health benefits.
Asante shows that residents of long-lived communities eat nearly identical diets.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Asante uzoq umr ko'rishni bitta mahsulotga emas, umumiy hayot tarzi — ijtimoiy aloqa, harakat, maqsad — bilan izohlaydi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: In a poem by the invented poet Lina Moravec, the speaker watches her grandmother knead bread early on a winter morning. The speaker notices the flour on her grandmother's wrists, the steady rhythm of her hands, and the warmth spreading from the oven through the cold kitchen. Throughout the poem, the speaker compares the kitchen to a small lit island in a dark sea, suggesting that her grandmother's work creates a place of comfort and safety.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best describes the grandmother's kitchen as presented in the text?
choices: It is portrayed as a lonely place the speaker wishes to leave.
It is portrayed as a warm, comforting refuge created by the grandmother's work.
It is portrayed as too cold for baking bread in winter.
It is portrayed as a noisy space filled with visiting relatives.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Oshxona qorong'i dengizdagi yorug' orolga qiyoslanadi, bu uning iliq va xavfsiz joy ekanini bildiradi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: Many people assume that languages with many speakers are the most likely to survive. Linguist Oyuna Batbayar points out that the number of speakers matters less than whether children are still learning a language at home. Some languages with hundreds of thousands of speakers are endangered because young people have switched to a more dominant language, while some languages with only a few thousand speakers remain stable because families continue to pass them on.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: According to the text, what does Batbayar consider most important for a language's survival?
choices: Whether children continue to learn the language at home.
Whether the language is taught in universities.
The total number of people who speak the language.
Whether the language has a written alphabet.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Batbayarning fikricha, tilning saqlanishi so'zlovchilar soniga emas, bolalar uni uyda o'rganishiga bog'liq.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: In a poem by the invented poet Amara Nwosu, the speaker recalls learning to swim in a river as a child. At first, the speaker thrashes against the current and sinks. Her uncle, standing nearby, tells her to stop fighting and lie back. When she does, she floats. In the final stanza, now an adult facing a difficult year, the speaker remembers her uncle's advice and writes that "some waters hold you only when you stop resisting them."
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the poem as described in the text?
choices: A childhood lesson about floating becomes guidance for handling hardship in adulthood.
The speaker still fears swimming because of a childhood accident.
The speaker's uncle was a professional swimming instructor.
The speaker regrets never having learned to swim properly.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Bolalikdagi suzish saboqi kattalikdagi qiyinchiliklarga qarshi kurashmaslik haqidagi hikmatga aylanadi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: Many museums have begun returning artifacts to the countries or communities from which they were taken. Critics argue that such returns could empty museums and deprive global audiences of important works. Curator Nadia Haddad, who has overseen several returns, disputes this. She notes that returned objects are often displayed in new museums in their places of origin, where they can be viewed alongside related sites and traditions. In some cases, she adds, the returning museum has received long-term loans of other works in exchange, so that its visitors still encounter objects from that culture.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Haddad believes museums should return every artifact in their collections.
Haddad admits that returns have emptied many museums of important works.
Haddad argues that returning artifacts need not reduce public access to them, contrary to critics' concerns.
Haddad claims that artifacts are better protected in large international museums.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Haddad tanqidchilarga javoban artefaktlarni qaytarish ularni ko'rish imkoniyatini kamaytirmasligini ta'kidlaydi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: Linguist Tomás Ribeiro studied whistled languages, in which speakers communicate by whistling the melody and rhythm of spoken words. Such languages exist in mountainous regions of Turkey, the Canary Islands, and parts of Mexico. Ribeiro found that they share a common function: whistles can travel several kilometers across valleys, much farther than shouted speech. In each region he studied, whistled speech developed where people worked far apart on steep terrain and needed a way to exchange messages without walking long distances.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Based on the text, what is the main reason whistled languages developed?
choices: They allowed speakers to keep messages secret from outsiders.
They replaced spoken languages that had disappeared in mountainous regions.
They allowed people separated by difficult terrain to communicate over long distances.
They were easier for children to learn than spoken languages.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Ribeironing xulosasiga ko'ra, hushtak tillari tik tog'li joylarda uzoqda ishlaydigan odamlar aloqa qilishi uchun paydo bo'lgan.

Central Ideas and Details.passage:
The following text is adapted from Willa Cather's 1913 novel O Pioneers! Alexandra Bergson has inherited her father's struggling farm on the Nebraska prairie.
When Alexandra looked out over the land, she did not see what her brothers saw—a harsh country that had broken their father. She saw a place that was waiting to be understood. For the first time, perhaps, since that land emerged from the waters of geologic ages, a human face was set toward it with love and yearning.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best describes Alexandra's view of the land as presented in the text?
choices: She shares her brothers' belief that the land is too harsh to farm.
She fears that the land will defeat her as it defeated her father.
She regards it with hope and affection, seeing possibility where others see hardship.
She values the land mainly for its geological history.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Aleksandra akalaridan farqli o'laroq yerga mehr va umid bilan qaraydi, uni qiyinchilik emas, imkoniyat deb biladi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: Coral reefs are threatened by rising ocean temperatures, which can cause corals to expel the algae that live in their tissues and provide them with food. Marine scientist Ruth Gates and her colleagues experimented with "assisted evolution": they collected corals that had survived heat waves, bred them in laboratories, and exposed their offspring to gradually warmer water. Some of the offspring proved more tolerant of heat than typical corals, raising hopes that such techniques could help restore damaged reefs.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Laboratory-bred corals cannot survive in the open ocean.
Researchers are testing whether breeding heat-tolerant corals could help reefs survive warming oceans.
Coral reefs have fully recovered from recent heat waves.
Algae are the main cause of damage to coral reefs.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Matn olimlar issiqqa chidamli marjonlarni ko'paytirish orqali riflarni saqlab qolish mumkinligini sinab ko'rayotganini tasvirlaydi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: When psychologist Harriet Oyelaran asked volunteers to memorize lists of words, she found that those who explained the words aloud to an imaginary student remembered more of them a week later than those who simply reread the list. Oyelaran suggests that preparing to teach forces learners to organize information and connect new ideas to what they already know. Rereading, by contrast, can create a false sense of familiarity without deepening understanding.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Based on the text, what is the main reason explaining words aloud improved memory?
choices: Preparing to teach requires learners to organize information and link it to prior knowledge.
Volunteers who explained words had more time to study.
Speaking aloud is faster than rereading a list silently.
Imaginary students asked questions that helped volunteers recall the words.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Oyelaranning fikricha, o'rgatishga tayyorlanish ma'lumotni tartibga solish va avvalgi bilimlar bilan bog'lashni talab qiladi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: Many psychologists have assumed that people make better decisions when they have more options to choose from. A series of studies by psychologist Sheena Iyengar suggested the opposite in some settings: shoppers offered twenty-four varieties of jam were less likely to buy any than those offered six. Later researchers attempting to repeat such experiments obtained mixed results, however, finding that the effect appeared only under certain conditions, such as when options were hard to compare or when shoppers lacked clear preferences.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Research suggests that too many options can discourage choosing, but later studies indicate this effect depends on specific conditions.
Later researchers showed that the number of options never affects decisions.
Iyengar proved that people always prefer fewer options.
Shoppers prefer jam to other products when given many choices.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Ko'p tanlov qaror qabul qilishni qiyinlashtirishi mumkin, ammo keyingi tadqiqotlar bu ta'sir faqat ma'lum sharoitlarda yuzaga kelishini ko'rsatgan.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: In a poem by the invented poet Rafael Ostrowski, the speaker describes a city bus at midnight. The passengers—a nurse finishing a shift, a baker heading to work, a student asleep against the window—never speak to one another. Yet the speaker notices small gestures: the nurse steadies the student's bag when the bus lurches, the baker nods at the driver. By the poem's end, the speaker calls the bus "a house with no walls, where strangers keep one another."
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the poem as described in the text?
choices: The speaker wishes the passengers would talk to one another more openly.
City buses at night are dangerous places for passengers traveling alone.
Night-shift workers are too exhausted to notice the people around them.
Even silent strangers can form a quiet sense of community through small acts of care.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: She'r notanish odamlar gaplashmasa ham kichik g'amxo'rlik harakatlari orqali jamoa hosil qilishini ko'rsatadi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage:
The following text is adapted from Mark Twain's 1876 novel The Adventures of Tom Sawyer. Tom has been told to whitewash a long fence on a Saturday.
Tom surveyed the fence, and all gladness left him. Thirty yards of board fence nine feet high. Life to him seemed hollow, and existence but a burden. He dipped his brush and passed it along the topmost plank; repeated the operation; did it again; compared the insignificant whitewashed streak with the far-reaching continent of unwhitewashed fence, and sat down discouraged.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best describes Tom's reaction to the task?
choices: He is angry at the person who built the fence.
He is excited to show his skill at painting.
He is confident he will finish the job quickly.
He feels overwhelmed and discouraged by how much work lies ahead of him.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Tom devorning kattaligini ko'rib ruhi tushadi va "discouraged" holda o'tirib qoladi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage:
The following text is adapted from Leo Tolstoy's 1886 story "How Much Land Does a Man Need?" Pahom, a peasant, has been offered as much land as he can walk around in one day.
Pahom walked on and on, and whenever he saw a good piece of land, he thought, "It would be a pity to leave that out." The farther he went, the better the land seemed, and he kept turning aside to include more. The sun was sinking, but still he could not bring himself to turn back toward the starting point.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best describes Pahom as presented in the text?
choices: He is content with the small amount of land he already owns.
He is driven by a desire for more land that overrides his caution.
He is too tired to continue walking toward the good land.
He is careful to return to the starting point before sunset.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Pahom har bir yaxshi yerni qo'shib olishni istab, quyosh botayotgan bo'lsa ham orqaga qaytolmaydi — bu uning ochko'zligini ko'rsatadi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: Many conservationists have argued that wolves reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park in 1995 caused a dramatic recovery of streamside willow trees by scaring elk away from rivers. Ecologist Tom Hobbs and his colleagues tested this idea by building fences that kept elk away from some willows. Even protected willows often failed to recover fully, because decades of heavy browsing had lowered water tables near streams. The researchers conclude that wolves may help, but restoring the park's rivers will require more than the return of a single predator.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Elk do not eat willow trees in Yellowstone National Park.
Research suggests that wolves alone cannot restore Yellowstone's willows, because long-term changes to streams also limit recovery.
Wolves have fully restored Yellowstone's rivers since 1995.
Fences are more effective than wolves at controlling elk populations everywhere.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Tadqiqot bo'rilar yordam berishi mumkinligini, lekin suv sathi pasaygani uchun tollarni tiklash yolg'iz bo'rilar bilan bo'lmasligini ko'rsatadi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: Honeyguides are small birds found in parts of Africa that lead people to wild bees' nests. When a honeyguide chirps and flies from tree to tree, people follow it until they find the nest. The people then break open the nest to collect honey, and the bird eats the leftover wax, which it cannot easily reach on its own. Researchers studying this partnership in Mozambique found that honeyguides respond especially to a special call that local honey hunters use.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: According to the text, what does the honeyguide gain from its partnership with people?
choices: Protection from predators while it searches for food.
Access to beeswax that it would have difficulty reaching by itself.
A safe place to build its own nest near villages.
Honey that people leave behind in special containers.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Matnda qush o'zi yeta olmaydigan mumni yeyishi aytilgan.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: In 2019, the town of Kamikatsu, Japan, announced that it was close to producing no trash at all. Residents sort their waste into more than forty categories, including separate bins for different kinds of plastic, paper, and metal. The town also runs a shop where people can drop off unwanted items and take others for free. Officials say the system took years to build, but it now recycles or reuses about 80 percent of the town's waste.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: According to the text, what is true about Kamikatsu?
choices: Its residents sort waste into many categories as part of an effort to reduce trash.
Its free shop sells used items at very low prices.
It became the first town in the world to produce no trash at all in 2019.
It built its recycling system in only a few months.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Aholi chiqindilarni qirqdan ortiq toifaga ajratadi. Shahar hali to'liq chiqindisiz emas, tizim esa yillar davomida qurilgan.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: Many desert plants store water in thick stems or leaves, but the welwitschia, which grows in the Namib Desert of southwestern Africa, has a different strategy. It produces only two leaves in its entire lifetime, which can exceed one thousand years. These long, ribbon-like leaves grow continuously from the base while their tips wither in the heat. Researchers believe the leaves absorb moisture from the fog that frequently rolls in from the Atlantic Ocean.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: According to the text, what is true about the welwitschia?
choices: It stores large amounts of water in its thick stem.
It sheds its leaves and grows new ones every year.
It produces just two leaves that keep growing throughout its long life.
It grows only near freshwater rivers in the Namib Desert.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Matnda welwitschia butun umri davomida faqat ikkita barg chiqarishi va ular to'xtovsiz o'sishi aytilgan.

Central Ideas and Details.passage:
The following text is adapted from Louisa May Alcott's 1868 novel Little Women. Jo, one of four sisters, is speaking.
"I like good strong words that mean something," replied Jo, catching her hat as it took a leap off her head, preparatory to flying away altogether. "I'm not going to be a lady just because other people say I should. I'd rather do the things I choose, and do them with all my might, than sit still and be admired for nothing."
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Based on the text, what is true about Jo?
choices: She values acting according to her own choices over meeting others' expectations of proper behavior.
She believes strong words should be avoided by young women.
She wishes to be admired by the people around her.
She is embarrassed that her hat keeps blowing away in public.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Jo boshqalarning kutganiga emas, o'z tanloviga ko'ra harakat qilishni afzal ko'radi: "I'd rather do the things I choose".

Central Ideas and Details.passage: Sociologist Mei-Ling Tran studied why some immigrant-founded restaurants in Toronto survived for decades while others closed within a few years. Popular accounts emphasize the quality of the food, but Tran found that food quality varied little between long-lasting and short-lived restaurants. What distinguished the survivors was that their owners had built networks with suppliers, landlords, and other business owners who offered credit, flexible rent, or advice during difficult periods. Tran concludes that restaurants' survival depends less on what happens in the kitchen than on relationships outside it.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Based on the text, what is the main reason some restaurants in Tran's study survived longer than others?
choices: They served higher-quality food than restaurants that closed.
Their owners had developed supportive relationships with people and businesses in their community.
They were located in neighborhoods with fewer competing restaurants.
Their owners had more experience working in professional kitchens.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Tranning xulosasiga ko'ra, restoranlarning uzoq yashashi ovqat sifatiga emas, tashqi aloqalar tarmog'iga bog'liq.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: In a poem by the invented poet Idris Calloway, the speaker describes repairing an old stone wall on his family's farm. For most of the poem, he lists the practical details of the job: which stones fit, how frost has pushed others loose, how his hands grow raw. Only in the final lines does he admit that his father built the wall and that he has not spoken to his father in years. The speaker ends by placing the last stone and saying that he "cannot tell whether I am mending the wall or the silence."
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the poem as described in the text?
choices: The speaker regrets inheriting a farm that requires so much physical labor.
The speaker learns that his father built the wall poorly and must fix his mistakes.
The physical task of repairing the wall becomes a way for the speaker to confront a broken relationship.
The poem mainly offers practical instructions for repairing stone walls.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: She'rning oxirida devorni ta'mirlash otasi bilan uzilgan munosabatni tiklashga urinish ramzi ekani ma'lum bo'ladi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: Cheetahs are famous for their speed, but a study led by zoologist Alan Wilson found that speed is not what makes their hunts successful. Using collars that recorded the movements of wild cheetahs in Botswana, Wilson's team discovered that the animals rarely reached top speed during hunts. Instead, their success depended on rapid acceleration and on the ability to slow down and turn sharply as prey changed direction.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: According to the text, what did Wilson's team discover about cheetahs?
choices: They rarely succeed in catching prey that changes direction.
Their hunting success depends more on acceleration and agility than on top speed.
They reach their highest speeds most often while hunting.
They hunt more successfully in Botswana than in other regions.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Tadqiqot gepardlarning muvaffaqiyati eng yuqori tezlikka emas, balki tezlanish va keskin burilishga bog'liqligini ko'rsatgan.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: When the city of Medellín, Colombia, built cable cars connecting hillside neighborhoods to the downtown metro system, planners mainly wanted to shorten residents' commutes. The trip that once took more than an hour by bus and on foot now takes about fifteen minutes. Researchers later found additional effects: new libraries and parks were built near cable car stations, and residents reported feeling more connected to the rest of the city.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Medellín's cable cars shortened commutes and also produced broader benefits for hillside neighborhoods.
Medellín's cable cars replaced the city's metro system.
Residents of hillside neighborhoods opposed the construction of cable cars.
Libraries and parks were the main reason the cable cars were built.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Kanat yo'llari yo'l vaqtini qisqartirgan va qo'shimcha foyda — kutubxona, park va bog'liqlik hissini — keltirgan.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: In a poem by the invented poet Soraya Haleem, the speaker describes the first snowfall of the year. She notices how the snow covers the muddy streets, the broken fence, and the pile of old tires behind the garage, making everything look clean and new. The speaker says the snow "forgives the town for one white morning."
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best describes how the snow is presented in the poem?
choices: It temporarily makes an untidy town look fresh and beautiful.
It causes damage to fences and buildings in the town.
It frightens the speaker because it arrives unexpectedly.
It melts quickly and makes the streets muddier.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Qor iflos va eski narsalarni yopib, shaharni bir tonggina toza va yangi ko'rsatadi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage:
The following text is adapted from George Eliot's 1871–1872 novel Middlemarch. The narrator reflects on Dorothea Brooke, a young woman eager to do great things.
Her full nature spent itself in channels which had no great name on the earth. But the effect of her being on those around her was incalculably diffusive: for the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts; and that things are not so ill with you and me as they might have been is half owing to the number who lived faithfully a hidden life.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Dorothea's life was hidden because she avoided contact with other people.
Dorothea regretted that she was never able to accomplish anything meaningful.
Only people whose deeds are recorded in history truly improve the world.
Although Dorothea never became famous, her quiet influence contributed to the good of the world.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Narrator Doroteya mashhur bo'lmasa ham, uning ko'rinmas yaxshi ishlari dunyoga ta'sir qilganini ta'kidlaydi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage:
The following text is adapted from Kate Chopin's 1894 short story "The Story of an Hour." Mrs. Mallard has just received news of her husband's death.
There would be no one to live for her during those coming years; she would live for herself. There would be no powerful will bending hers in that blind persistence with which men and women believe they have a right to impose a private will upon a fellow-creature. She said it over and over under her breath: "Free, free, free!"
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best describes Mrs. Mallard's feelings as presented in the text?
choices: She is afraid of being alone without her husband's guidance.
She is angry that others imposed the news on her so suddenly.
She feels a growing sense of freedom at the thought of living for herself.
She is overwhelmed with grief and cannot imagine her future.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Missis Mallard o'zi uchun yashash imkoniyatini his qilib "Free, free, free!" deb takrorlaydi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: Arctic terns make one of the longest migrations of any animal. Each year, they fly from their breeding grounds in the Arctic to the coast of Antarctica and back again, a round trip that can exceed 70,000 kilometers. Because they follow the summer between the two poles, Arctic terns likely see more daylight than any other creature on Earth.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Based on the text, why do Arctic terns likely see more daylight than any other creature?
choices: They migrate shorter distances than other birds.
They spend time near both poles during each region's summer.
They live year-round near the equator.
They fly only during the daytime and rest at night.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Qutb qarqarlari ikki qutb o'rtasida yozni ta'qib qilgani uchun eng ko'p kunduzgi yorug'likni ko'radi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: Volunteers in the city of Leeds planted fruit trees along several public walking paths in 2015. The organizers hoped that residents would pick the apples, plums, and pears for free. Over the next few years, they noticed an unexpected benefit: neighbors who had never spoken before began meeting at the trees during harvest season, trading recipes and helping one another reach high branches. Organizers now describe the project as much about building friendships as about providing food.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Fruit trees grow better along walking paths than in private gardens.
The organizers mainly wanted to teach residents how to cook with fruit.
Residents of Leeds were unwilling to pick fruit from public trees.
A project to plant public fruit trees also brought neighbors together in unexpected ways.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Loyiha oziq-ovqat bilan birga qo'shnilar o'rtasida do'stlik ham yaratgan — bu matnning asosiy g'oyasi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: Researchers have long debated why the Classic Maya cities of the southern lowlands were largely abandoned around 900 CE. Some point to severe droughts recorded in lake sediments; others emphasize warfare between rival cities. Archaeologist Tanvir Hossain argues that treating these as competing explanations is a mistake. In his view, drought reduced harvests, food shortages intensified conflict between cities, and warfare in turn disrupted the trade networks and farming systems that might have helped communities recover.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Hossain argues that drought, not warfare, was the only cause of the Maya decline.
Hossain claims that Maya trade networks were stronger after 900 CE.
Hossain suggests that drought and warfare worked together to cause the abandonment of Maya cities, rather than being separate explanations.
Hossain shows that lake sediments provide no evidence of drought.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Hossain qurg'oqchilik va urushni raqobatdosh emas, bir-birini kuchaytirgan omillar deb hisoblaydi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: Engineers designing earthquake-resistant buildings once focused mainly on making structures as rigid as possible. More recent designs, such as those promoted by structural engineer Yuki Tanabe, take a different approach. Tanabe's buildings rest on flexible bearings made of layered rubber and steel, which allow the ground to shift beneath them while the structure above moves far less. Tanabe acknowledges that such systems cost more to install, but she argues that they reduce long-term expenses by limiting damage that would otherwise require extensive repairs.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Tanabe believes that rigid buildings are cheaper to repair after earthquakes.
Tanabe has shown that rubber bearings prevent all earthquake damage.
Tanabe favors flexible foundations over rigid designs, arguing that their higher initial cost is offset by reduced damage.
Tanabe argues that engineers should avoid building in earthquake-prone areas.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Tanabe moslashuvchan poydevorlarni afzal ko'radi va dastlabki yuqori xarajat keyinchalik ta'mirlash xarajatlarini kamaytirish orqali qoplanadi deb hisoblaydi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage:
The following text is adapted from Thomas Hardy's 1878 novel The Return of the Native. The narrator describes Egdon Heath, a wide, wild moorland.
The heath was a place perfectly accordant with man's nature—neither ghastly, hateful, nor ugly; neither commonplace, unmeaning, nor tame; but, like man, slighted and enduring. Civilization was its enemy; and ever since the beginning of vegetation its soil had worn the same antique brown dress. It had a lonely face, suggesting tragical possibilities.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best describes the heath as presented in the text?
choices: It is an ugly wasteland that the narrator hopes will be developed.
It is a timeless, unchanging landscape whose somber endurance mirrors human nature.
It is a landscape that changes dramatically with each season.
It is a beautiful, cheerful place that welcomes visitors.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Narrator botqoqlikni insonga o'xshash — e'tiborsiz qolgan, ammo bardoshli va o'zgarmas deb ta'riflaydi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage:
The following text is adapted from Edith Wharton's 1905 novel The House of Mirth. Lily Bart, a young woman in New York high society, is observing her friend Selden's modest apartment.
Lily looked about her with a sigh. How delicious to have a place like this all to oneself! What a miserable thing it is to be a woman! She knew that she would never be content in such a room for long; she had been bred to want larger rooms, finer things. Yet for the moment its plainness struck her as a kind of freedom she had never been allowed.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best describes Lily's reaction to the apartment?
choices: She is disgusted by the plainness of the apartment and wants to leave immediately.
She is drawn to the independence it represents even though she knows her upbringing would make her dissatisfied with it.
She envies Selden because his apartment is larger and finer than her own home.
She plans to give up her social position so that she can live in a similar apartment.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Lily kvartirani erkinlik ramzi sifatida ko'radi, ammo tarbiyasi tufayli unda uzoq qanoat qila olmasligini biladi. Bu ikki tomonlama munosabatni faqat to'g'ri javob aks ettiradi.

Central Ideas and Details.passage: Engineers once assumed that electric scooters in cities would mainly replace car trips, reducing traffic and emissions. A study by transportation researcher Anneke de Vries in several European cities found a more complicated pattern. Most scooter trips replaced walking or public transit rather than car journeys, and the scooters' short lifespans meant their manufacturing emissions were significant. De Vries notes, though, that newer, more durable scooter models and programs that link scooters to train stations could make them a greener option in the future.
Central Ideas and Details.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: De Vries recommends banning e-scooters from all city streets.
E-scooters have so far done less to reduce emissions than expected, though design and planning changes could improve their impact.
E-scooters have greatly reduced car traffic in European cities.
Public transit produces more emissions than e-scooters do.
Central Ideas and Details.expl: Skuterlar kutilgandek emissiyani kamaytirmagan, ammo de Vries kelajakda bardoshliroq modellar va rejalashtirish vaziyatni yaxshilashi mumkinligini aytadi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Marine biologist Keiko Arai studies how hermit crabs select new shells when they outgrow their old ones. Many researchers have assumed that crabs prefer shells whose color matches their surroundings, which would help them avoid predators. Arai, however, hypothesizes that shell weight, not color, is the main factor in a crab's choice, since a heavy shell slows a crab down and increases the energy it must spend while foraging.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Arai's hypothesis?
choices: When offered shells that differed only in color, crabs chose among them at random, but when offered shells that differed only in weight, crabs consistently chose the lighter ones.
Crabs living on dark volcanic sand were more often found in dark shells than crabs living on pale coral sand.
Heavier shells were found to protect crabs from predators more effectively than lighter shells did.
Crabs that had recently changed shells spent more time foraging than crabs that had not changed shells in several weeks.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Arai rang emas, og'irlik muhim deb hisoblaydi; qisqichbaqalar rangga befarq, lekin doimo yengil chig'anoqni tanlashi aynan shuni tasdiqlaydi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Volcanologist Aroha Ngata studies eruptions on New Zealand's North Island. She hypothesizes that small earthquakes clustered at shallow depths beneath a volcano are a more reliable warning sign of an eruption within the following month than are changes in the volcano's gas emissions. Predicting eruptions is difficult because volcanoes can show signs of unrest for years without erupting. Ngata compiled records of both earthquakes and gas measurements for several volcanoes over two decades.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ngata's hypothesis?
choices: Shallow earthquake clusters were recorded at several volcanoes that have not erupted in centuries.
Instruments that measure gas emissions are more expensive to maintain than seismometers.
Gas emissions from the volcano varied widely from season to season.

Of the eruptions recorded over two decades, most were preceded within a month by shallow earthquake clusters, whereas sharp changes in gas emissions preceded fewer than half of them and often occurred without any eruption following.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Gipoteza ikki belgini taqqoslaydi; zilzila guruhlari ko'p otilishlardan oldin kelgani, gaz o'zgarishlari esa kamroq va ko'pincha noto'g'ri signal bergani aynan shuni tasdiqlaydi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: In many species of cichlid fish, males guard nests while females forage. Biologist Rehema Mushi observed that in Lake Tanganyika, males of one cichlid species guard nests more aggressively when many rival males are nearby. She hypothesizes that this increase in aggression is a response to the risk that rivals will fertilize eggs in the nest, rather than a response to the risk that predators will eat the eggs.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Mushi's hypothesis?
choices: Males guarded more aggressively in areas of the lake where egg-eating predators were abundant.
Males that guarded more aggressively had nests with more surviving eggs than males that guarded less aggressively.

Males guarded most aggressively when rival males were near the nest during the brief period when females were laying eggs, and their aggression declined sharply once all eggs had been fertilized, even though egg-eating predators remained just as common.
Males of the species were larger, on average, than males of related species that do not guard nests.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Tajovuz faqat urug'lantirish davrida kuchli bo'lib, yirtqichlar soni o'zgarmasa ham keyin pasaygani uning raqiblar urug'lantirishi xavfiga javob ekanini ko'rsatadi. B variant ikkala gipotezaga ham mos keladi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Economist Tomás Ribeiro has studied small farmers' markets in Portugal. He hypothesizes that when a market adds a mobile payment option, sales rise mainly because younger shoppers, who rarely carry cash, begin visiting the market, rather than because existing customers spend more per visit. Mobile payment systems have spread rapidly across Portuguese towns in recent years, and many market organizers have adopted them hoping to attract new business. To examine the effect, Ribeiro collected sales records and shopper surveys from several markets.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Ribeiro's hypothesis?
choices: Markets that did not introduce mobile payment saw no change in total sales over the same period.
After mobile payment was introduced, the number and ages of shoppers stayed about the same, but the average amount each returning customer spent per visit increased sharply.
After mobile payment was introduced, the share of shoppers under age thirty roughly doubled.
Vendors reported that setting up mobile payment took less time than they had expected.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Agar xaridorlar soni va yoshi o'zgarmay, faqat har bir tashrifdagi xarajat oshgan bo'lsa, o'sish yosh xaridorlar hisobidan emas, balki mavjud mijozlar hisobidan bo'lgan bo'ladi; bu gipotezani zaiflashtiradi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Economist Yerlan Abenov studied villages in Kazakhstan that received new paved roads. Before the roads were built, the journey to the nearest city took most of a day. He hypothesizes that the roads increased household incomes mainly by allowing farmers to sell their produce in distant city markets, where prices are higher, rather than by lowering the cost of goods that villagers buy.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Abenov's hypothesis?
choices: After the roads were built, the share of village produce sold in city markets rose substantially, while the prices villagers paid for purchased goods changed very little.
After the roads were built, the prices villagers paid for fuel and building materials dropped considerably.
Villages that received roads were, on average, larger than villages that did not.
After the roads were built, villagers traveled to the city more often to visit relatives.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Mahsulotning shahar bozorlarida sotilishi oshgani, xarid narxlari esa deyarli o'zgarmagani daromad o'sishi sotuv hisobidan ekanini ko'rsatadi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Historian Leopold Varga studies the spread of printed books in sixteenth-century Hungary. Some scholars attribute the rapid rise in literacy in certain towns to the arrival of printing presses. Varga hypothesizes instead that literacy rates in those towns had already begun climbing before presses arrived and that printers deliberately chose to settle in towns where a reading public already existed.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Varga's hypothesis?
choices: The first printers in Hungary had generally trained in German cities.
Towns that acquired printing presses had higher literacy rates in 1600 than towns that did not.

Parish records show that the proportion of townspeople able to sign their names in the towns that later acquired presses was already increasing for several decades before the first press was established there, faster than in comparable towns that never acquired one.
After printing presses arrived, the number of books owned by townspeople increased greatly.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Pres kelishidan oldin savodxonlik allaqachon o'sayotgani matbaachilar tayyor o'quvchilar bor joyni tanlaganini ko'rsatadi. B variant qaysi biri avval kelganini ajratmaydi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage:
The following text is adapted from Leonora Vance's 1909 novel The Lamplighter's Daughter. Maud, a young woman working in her father's bookshop, has been asked to manage the shop while he travels. The shop is small, but it has a loyal circle of customers, and Maud has never before been left in charge of it for more than an afternoon.

A literary critic claims that Maud feels both excitement and anxiety about the responsibility she has been given.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which quotation from The Lamplighter's Daughter most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "She unlocked the door that first morning with a thrill she could hardly contain, yet she counted the coins in the drawer three times before she dared to open the shutters."
"Maud had always preferred the poetry shelves to the tidy rows of accounting books her father kept behind the counter."
"The shop smelled, as it always had, of old paper and the faint smoke of the stove in the back room."
"Her father had written that the weather in the north was fair and that he expected to return by the end of the month."
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: To'g'ri iqtibosda 'hayajon' (thrill) va xavotir (tangalarni uch marta sanash) birga ko'rsatilgan, bu da'voning ikkala qismini tasvirlaydi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage:
The following text is adapted from Josephine Harcourt's 1895 novel The Hollow Crown Inn. Walter, the innkeeper, has just learned that a new hotel will open across the road. The inn has served travelers on the road for generations, and Walter has always taken pride in its reputation.

A critic claims that Walter responds to the news with a show of indifference that conceals his worry.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which quotation from The Hollow Crown Inn most effectively illustrates the critic's claim?
choices: "The new hotel, it was said, would have electric lamps in every room and a dining hall large enough for a hundred guests."
"'A hotel?' cried Walter. 'Then I am ruined, and my father's work is undone!'"
"Walter had kept the inn for twenty years, and in that time he had never once closed its doors."
"'Let them build,' Walter said with a shrug, returning to his ledger; but the guests noticed that he wiped the same clean glass for nearly an hour, glancing again and again toward the window."
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: To'g'ri iqtibosda Walter befarqlik ko'rsatadi (yelka qisadi), lekin bir stakanni soatlab artishi yashirin xavotirni bildiradi. B iqtibosda xavotir ochiq ifodalangan, yashirilmagan.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage:
The following text is adapted from Cordelia Marsh's 1898 novel The Unwritten Page. Theodora, a novelist, is being interviewed about her newest book, which critics have praised extravagantly. The book has sold more copies in its first month than all of her previous novels combined.

A scholar argues that Theodora regards public acclaim as irrelevant to her own judgment of her work.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which quotation from The Unwritten Page most effectively illustrates the scholar's argument?
choices: "She had written the book in a single winter, rising before dawn each day to work by candlelight."
"'I never read what the papers say,' she remarked, 'for I cannot bear to be told I have failed.'"
"'I confess the reviews have pleased me,' she said, 'though I cannot think I deserve half of what they say.'"
"'They may call it a masterpiece if they like,' she said, pouring the tea. 'I know which chapters are hollow, and their applause will not fill them.'"
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: To'g'ri iqtibosda Teodora maqtovlarga qaramay qaysi boblar zaifligini o'zi biladi; bu uning bahosi olqishlarga bog'liq emasligini ko'rsatadi. B variant tanqiddan qo'rqishni bildiradi, befarqlikni emas.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Botanist Priya Raman investigated why some populations of wild strawberry plants produce far more runners (horizontal stems that grow into new plants) than others. Raman hypothesizes that plants growing in shaded forest understories produce more runners than plants in open meadows because runners allow a plant to "search" for patches of sunlight. To investigate, she collected plants from both types of habitat.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Raman's hypothesis?
choices: When genetically identical strawberry plants were grown under artificial shade and in full light, the shaded plants produced significantly more runners, and those runners tended to root in brighter spots.
Runners produced by meadow plants were, on average, slightly longer than runners produced by forest plants.
Strawberry plants in open meadows produced larger and sweeter fruit than plants in forest understories.
Forest understory plants of many species grow more slowly than the same species grown in meadows.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Soya ostidagi bir xil o'simliklar ko'proq yer ustidan o'suvchi poya chiqarib, yorug' joylarda ildiz otishi quyosh nurini 'izlash' g'oyasini bevosita qo'llab-quvvatlaydi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Neuroscientist Adaeze Okafor hypothesizes that the improvement in memory commonly observed after a night's sleep depends specifically on deep, slow-wave sleep rather than on the total number of hours slept. It is well established that people tend to remember newly learned information better after sleeping than after an equal period of wakefulness. But sleep consists of several stages, and researchers disagree about which ones matter most. Okafor designed a sleep-laboratory study to find out.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Okafor's hypothesis?
choices: Participants who slept nine hours remembered more word pairs than participants who slept five hours.
Participants reported feeling more alert after nights with more slow-wave sleep.

Participants whose slow-wave sleep was selectively interrupted by gentle sounds, without reducing their total sleep time, showed much smaller memory gains than participants whose sleep was undisturbed.
Slow-wave sleep makes up a larger portion of the night in children than in older adults.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Umumiy uyqu vaqti o'zgarmagan holda faqat chuqur uyqu buzilganda xotira kam yaxshilangani chuqur uyquning o'zi muhimligini ko'rsatadi. A variant umumiy vaqtni chuqur uyqudan ajratmaydi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Plant physiologist Anjali Mehta studies desert plants that open their stomata (pores for gas exchange) only at night. Mehta hypothesizes that in one species, this nighttime opening is controlled by an internal circadian clock rather than being a direct response to the drop in temperature that occurs after sunset. This nighttime pattern helps the plants conserve water, since less water evaporates in cool night air. Mehta grew the plants in growth chambers where light and temperature could be precisely controlled.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Mehta's hypothesis?
choices: When plants were kept under constant temperature and constant dim light for several days, their stomata continued to open and close on a roughly twenty-four-hour cycle matching the previous day-night pattern.
When nighttime temperatures were artificially raised, the plants' stomata opened later than usual.
Plants of this species lose less water per day than most plants of similar size in wetter climates.
The plants' stomata opened more widely on cool nights than on warm nights.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Harorat va yorug'lik doimiy bo'lsa ham og'izchalar 24 soatlik siklda ochilib-yopilishi ichki soat mavjudligini ko'rsatadi. B va D variantlar haroratga javobni ko'rsatadi, bu raqib tushuntirishni qo'llaydi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Linguist Dilnoza Yusupova hypothesizes that children who grow up speaking two languages at home are better than monolingual children at ignoring irrelevant information, because constantly switching between languages trains the brain to suppress whichever language is not currently needed. Researchers have long debated whether bilingualism affects thinking skills beyond language itself. To test her idea, Yusupova plans to compare children from similar neighborhoods and schools in Samarkand.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Yusupova's hypothesis?
choices: Bilingual children knew fewer words in each of their two languages than monolingual children knew in their one language.

On a task requiring participants to name the color of ink in which a word is printed while ignoring the word itself, bilingual children made fewer errors than monolingual children of the same age and background.
Monolingual children read aloud faster than bilingual children did.
Parents of bilingual children reported spending more time reading to their children than parents of monolingual children did.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Rangni aytib, so'zni e'tiborsiz qoldirish vazifasi keraksiz ma'lumotni bostirish qobiliyatini o'lchaydi; bilingvallarning kamroq xato qilishi gipotezani tasdiqlaydi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Marine ecologist Lucía Ferreyra studies kelp forests off the coast of Chile. She hypothesizes that the recovery of sea otter populations in a region leads to healthier kelp forests because otters eat sea urchins, which graze heavily on kelp. Sea urchins can strip large areas of seafloor bare of kelp when their numbers are not controlled. Ferreyra surveyed sites along the coast where otters had returned and sites where they had not.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Ferreyra's hypothesis?
choices: In areas where otter populations recovered, sea urchin numbers remained unchanged, and kelp cover increased only in areas that also experienced cooler water temperatures, whether or not otters were present.
Kelp forests provide habitat for many species of fish.
Sea otters in the region were observed eating crabs and clams as well as sea urchins.
In areas where otter populations recovered, sea urchin numbers fell and kelp cover increased.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Agar otterlar tiklangan joylarda tipratikanlar soni o'zgarmasa va kelp faqat sovuq suvda ko'paysa, otterlar sabab ekanligi haqidagi gipoteza zaiflashadi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Economists have observed that cities with more coffee shops tend to have more new technology companies. Economist Rafael Domínguez hypothesizes that coffee shops actively contribute to the formation of technology companies by providing informal spaces where potential cofounders meet, rather than simply being more common in places that already attract young, educated workers. Domínguez gathered data on business openings in neighborhoods across several Spanish cities.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Domínguez's hypothesis?
choices: Among neighborhoods with similar numbers of young, educated residents, those where coffee shops opened subsequently saw more new technology companies founded, and founders frequently reported having first met their partners in those shops.
Young, educated workers are more likely than other groups to visit coffee shops regularly.
The number of coffee shops in major cities has grown steadily over the past twenty years.
Cities with more technology companies also tend to have more restaurants and gyms.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Aholi tarkibi o'xshash hududlarda kofexonalar ochilgach kompaniyalar ko'proq tashkil topgani va asoschilar u yerda tanishgani korrelyatsiyadan tashqari sabab bog'liqlikni ko'rsatadi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage:
The following text is from Harriet Oakley's 1897 short story "The Orchard Gate." Silas, an elderly farmer, has refused for years to sell his land to a railway company. The company has offered him several times what the land is worth, and his neighbors consider his stubbornness a mystery.

A student claims that Silas's refusal to sell stems from his attachment to memories of his late wife.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which quotation from "The Orchard Gate" most effectively illustrates the student's claim?
choices: "The railway men came twice each year, and each time their offer was a little larger than before."
"Every spring he walked to the pear tree she had planted the year they married, and he would say aloud, as if she could hear, that no iron rail would ever cross her roots."
"Silas kept his accounts in a battered notebook and knew to the penny what each harvest was worth."
"His neighbors had sold their farms long ago and moved to the town, where the work was easier and the pay more certain."
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: To'g'ri iqtibos Silasning rad etishini marhum xotini ekkan nok daraxti bilan bevosita bog'laydi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage:
The following text is from Lavinia Crane's 1902 poem sequence Letters from the Salt Road. The speaker, a woman traveling alone across a desert, addresses her absent brother. The sequence consists of twelve poems written as letters, each describing a different stage of the journey. In each, she describes the landscape in close detail.

A scholar argues that the speaker finds the desert's emptiness liberating rather than frightening.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which quotation from Letters from the Salt Road most effectively illustrates the scholar's argument?
choices: "You would laugh, brother, to see me in these borrowed boots, / the camel stubborn and the guide asleep."
"The sand is pale as flour and the wind is dry; / I count the days until the caravan turns home."
"At night the silence presses on my ears / until I long for any voice at all, even a stranger's."
"Here there are no walls to tell me where to stand, / and I have never breathed so freely as beneath this sky that asks nothing of me."
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: To'g'ri iqtibosda so'zlovchi devorlar yo'qligi va erkin nafas olishini aytadi, bu bo'shliqni ozodlik sifatida his qilishni ko'rsatadi. C variant esa qo'rquv/yolg'izlikni bildiradi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Paleontologist Birgit Halvorsen studies a small feathered dinosaur whose fossils have been found in northern China. The animal was about the size of a chicken, and its fossils preserve impressions of feathers in remarkable detail. Some researchers have argued that its feathers were used mainly for display to attract mates. Halvorsen hypothesizes that the feathers served primarily to keep the animal warm.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Halvorsen's hypothesis?
choices: Fossils of the dinosaur have been found in rock layers that formed during a relatively cool period.
Juvenile specimens had almost no feathers, while adults developed elaborate, brightly patterned feathers only on their tails and forelimbs, leaving much of the body sparsely covered.
The feathers of the dinosaur resembled the downy feathers of modern birds in structure.
Related dinosaurs that lived in warmer regions had fewer feathers than this species did.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Yosh hayvonlarda (issiqlik eng zarur bo'lganda) patlar yo'qligi va kattalarda faqat dum va oldingi oyoqlarda yorqin patlar bo'lishi ko'rgazma vazifasini ko'rsatadi, issiqlik saqlashni emas.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Urban planner Marcus Oyelaran studied neighborhoods in Lagos where trees were planted along streets. He hypothesizes that street trees lower the surface temperature of nearby sidewalks primarily by providing shade rather than by releasing water vapor through their leaves. Trees can cool their surroundings in two ways: their canopies block sunlight, and their leaves release water that evaporates and absorbs heat. Oyelaran measured sidewalk temperatures on dozens of streets during the hot season.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Oyelaran's hypothesis?
choices: Sidewalks under dense tree canopies were several degrees cooler than sidewalks with no trees nearby.
Sidewalks next to trees whose canopies had been pruned to cast almost no shade remained nearly as cool as sidewalks under full, unpruned canopies.
Residents of tree-lined streets reported spending more time walking outdoors.
Trees planted along streets required more frequent watering during the dry season than trees in parks.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Soya deyarli yo'q bo'lganda ham yo'lak salqin qolsa, sovutishning asosiy sababi soya emasligi ko'rinadi, bu gipotezani zaiflashtiradi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Anthropologist Sione Taufa hypothesizes that on certain Pacific islands, the tradition of communal fishing persisted longer in villages with fewer private motorboats, because owning a motorboat allowed families to fish independently and reduced their reliance on group effort. Communal fishing, in which a large group works together using shared nets, was once common throughout the region, but it has disappeared from many villages over the past century. Taufa gathered historical records from dozens of villages.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Taufa's hypothesis?
choices: Across the islands studied, villages where communal fishing ended earliest were those in which motorboat ownership had spread most rapidly, even when the villages were similar in size and distance from markets.
Communal fishing trips typically involved between ten and thirty people.
Villages with communal fishing traditions also held more community festivals.
Motorboats on the islands were most often used for transporting goods between islands.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Motorli qayiqlar tez tarqalgan qishloqlarda jamoaviy baliq ovi erta tugagani, boshqa omillar o'xshash bo'lgan holda, gipotezani qo'llab-quvvatlaydi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage:
The following text is from Marguerite Delacroix-Hill's 1901 novel The Long Field. Samuel, a farmer's son, has returned home after years of study abroad. His family are farmers who have never traveled farther than the market town, and they greet him with a celebration.

A critic claims that Samuel feels estranged from his family even as he tries to reconnect with them.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which quotation from The Long Field most effectively illustrates the critic's claim?
choices: "Samuel had written home faithfully every month, describing the lecture halls and libraries of the city."
"He praised his mother's bread and asked after the neighbors by name, and soon it was as if he had never been away."
"The farm looked smaller than he remembered, the barn roof patched in three places with mismatched boards."

"He praised his mother's bread and asked after the neighbors by name, but when his brothers laughed at a joke about the harvest, he laughed a moment too late, like a man translating from a language he had once known."
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: To'g'ri iqtibosda Samuel yaqinlashishga harakat qiladi (non maqtaydi, qo'shnilarni so'raydi), lekin kulgiga kech qo'shilishi begonalashganini ko'rsatadi; da'voning ikkala qismi mavjud.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Zoologist Hana Kowalczyk studies song sparrows. She hypothesizes that young male song sparrows learn their songs mainly by listening to neighboring adult males during their first spring, rather than by inheriting the songs genetically from their fathers. Song sparrows are known for singing distinctive songs that vary from one region to another, and researchers have long asked how young birds acquire them. Kowalczyk tracked banded birds over several years.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Kowalczyk's hypothesis?
choices: Young males raised by their fathers but moved to a distant area before their first spring sang songs that closely matched those of their new neighbors, not those of their fathers.
Female song sparrows showed a preference for males that sang longer songs.
Adult male song sparrows sang most frequently in the early morning.
Young males whose fathers had large song repertoires tended to be larger in body size than other young males.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Yosh erkaklar otasining emas, yangi qo'shnilarining qo'shig'ini kuylashi qo'shiqni tinglash orqali o'rganishni ko'rsatadi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Materials scientist Gustav Ekdahl hypothesizes that ancient Roman concrete in seaside structures became stronger over time because seawater seeping into the concrete reacted with volcanic ash in the mixture to form new minerals that filled cracks. Many Roman harbors and seawalls built nearly two thousand years ago remain intact today, while much modern concrete placed in seawater deteriorates within decades. Ekdahl analyzed samples taken from several ancient structures.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ekdahl's hypothesis?
choices: Many Roman harbor structures are still standing today.
Roman builders often used volcanic ash from the region around Mount Vesuvius.
Modern concrete exposed to seawater tends to crack and weaken within decades.

Samples of Roman harbor concrete contained mineral crystals in their cracks that form only when seawater reacts with volcanic ash, and these crystals were absent from Roman concrete of the same recipe used inland.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Faqat dengiz suvi bilan reaksiyada hosil bo'ladigan kristallar dengiz bo'yidagi betonda bor, quruqlikdagisida yo'qligi gipotezadagi mexanizmni tasdiqlaydi. A variant mustahkamlikni ko'rsatadi, lekin sababini emas.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Cognitive scientist Mireille Dubois hypothesizes that infants' preference for looking at faces is not present at birth but develops through early visual experience with the people around them. Other researchers argue that newborns are born with a built-in tendency to attend to face-like patterns. The debate is difficult to settle because babies begin seeing faces almost immediately after birth. Researchers have therefore tried to test newborns as early as possible.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Dubois's hypothesis?
choices: Infants aged six months looked longer at their mothers' faces than at strangers' faces.
Newborns' vision is blurry, and they see most clearly at a distance of about thirty centimeters.

Newborns tested within an hour of birth, before they had seen any faces clearly, turned their heads to follow a simple pattern of three dots arranged like eyes and a mouth more than the same dots arranged upside down.
Infants who spent more time with caregivers in their first months recognized familiar faces sooner.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Hech qanday yuzni ko'rmagan chaqaloqlarning yuzsimon naqshni afzal ko'rishi bu moyillik tug'ma ekanini ko'rsatadi va tajriba orqali rivojlanadi degan gipotezani zaiflashtiradi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage:
The following text is adapted from Arthur Penhallow's 1904 novel The Glass Harbor. Nell, a lighthouse keeper's daughter, has just been offered a place at a school in the city. The offer arrives in a letter from a distant aunt, who promises to pay all of Nell's expenses.

In the novel, Penhallow portrays Nell as reluctant to leave the coast despite the opportunity.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which quotation from The Glass Harbor most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "She folded the letter and set it beneath the lamp, and for three nights she climbed the tower to watch the sea as though she meant to memorize every wave before it could be taken from her."
"Nell read the letter aloud to her father, pronouncing each word with great care."
"The city school was known for its library, which held more books than Nell had seen in her whole life."
"Her father trimmed the wick at dusk and polished the great lens each morning, as his own father had done."
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Nellning har kecha dengizni 'yodlab olish' uchun minoraga chiqishi uning qirg'oqni tark etishni istamasligini ko'rsatadi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage:
The following text is adapted from Cyrus Wendell's 1899 novel The Surveyor's Map. Eliza, a surveyor's assistant, has discovered an error in a map her employer has already submitted to the government. Mr. Hale, her employer, hired Eliza years earlier when other surveyors refused to take on a woman as an assistant.

In the novel, Wendell presents Eliza as torn between loyalty to her employer and her commitment to accuracy.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which quotation from The Surveyor's Map most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "Twice she took up her pen to write to the land office, and twice she laid it down, thinking of Mr. Hale's kindness in taking her on when no one else would; yet the false line on the map stared up at her like an accusation."
"Without a moment's hesitation, Eliza wrote to the land office to report the mistake."
"The map showed the river bending sharply to the east, though in truth it turned west just beyond the ridge."
"Eliza had always been quick with figures, and Mr. Hale often said she could measure a field more precisely than he could."
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: To'g'ri iqtibosda Eliza ish beruvchiga minnatdorlik va xaritadagi xato orasida ikkilanadi. B variant ikkilanishni emas, qat'iy harakatni ko'rsatadi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Ecologist Tariq Hussaini studies pikas, small mammals that live on rocky mountain slopes in Central Asia. Pikas do not hibernate; instead, they rely on piles of stored plants and the insulation of snow to survive the winter. Pikas at lower elevations have disappeared from many sites. Hussaini hypothesizes that the main cause is not summer heat directly harming the animals but the loss of insulating winter snowpack, which leaves pikas exposed to lethal cold during winter.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Hussaini's hypothesis?
choices: Pikas are known to be highly sensitive to high temperatures and can die after brief exposure to heat.
The sites where pikas disappeared had experienced the largest increases in summer temperatures.
Pikas at higher elevations collect and store more vegetation for the winter than those at lower elevations.
The sites where pikas disappeared had experienced significantly thinner winter snow cover in recent decades but no greater increase in summer temperatures than the sites where pikas persisted.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Pikalar yo'qolgan joylarda qor qoplami yupqalashgan, lekin yozgi harorat boshqa joylardagidan ko'proq oshmagani asosiy sabab qish sovug'i ekanini ko'rsatadi. B va A variantlar raqib gipotezani qo'llaydi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Psychologist Ines Castellano hypothesizes that people remember information better when they explain it aloud to another person than when they simply reread it, because explaining forces them to organize the material and notice gaps in their understanding. Many students prepare for exams simply by rereading their notes or textbooks, a strategy that feels productive but may not be. Castellano designed an experiment with university students to compare study methods.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Castellano's hypothesis?
choices: Most students said they preferred studying alone rather than with a partner.
Students reported that rereading a passage felt less tiring than explaining it to a partner.
Students who read a passage in a quiet room scored higher than students who read it in a noisy room.
Students who spent twenty minutes explaining a passage to a partner scored higher on a test given a week later than students who spent the same twenty minutes rereading the passage.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Bir xil vaqt davomida tushuntirgan talabalarning keyingi testda yuqoriroq ball olishi tushuntirish xotirani yaxshilashini tasdiqlaydi.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Public health researcher Nadia Haddad hypothesizes that a text-message reminder system increased vaccination rates in a Jordanian city mainly by helping parents who intended to vaccinate their children but forgot appointments, rather than by persuading parents who had been reluctant to vaccinate. Before the program began, the city's childhood vaccination rate lagged behind the national average. The reminders were sent to parents two days before each scheduled appointment, and Haddad surveyed parents both before and after the program started.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Haddad's hypothesis?
choices: Vaccination rates in the city rose by about fifteen percent after the reminder system was introduced.

Surveys conducted before the program showed that most parents who later responded to the reminders had already planned to vaccinate their children, and the rate of missed appointments dropped sharply after reminders began.
Parents who described themselves as reluctant to vaccinate became much more likely to do so after receiving reminders.
The text messages were sent in both Arabic and English.
Command of Evidence (Textual).expl: Javob berganlar oldindan emlashni rejalashtirgan va o'tkazib yuborilgan uchrashuvlar kamaygani eslatmalar unutuvchan ota-onalarga yordam berganini ko'rsatadi. C variant gipotezaga zid.

Command of Evidence (Textual).passage: Musicologist Kiri Tawhai studies a collection of work songs sung by nineteenth-century whalers. The songs were used to coordinate tasks such as hauling ropes and raising anchors. Previous scholars assumed the songs were composed on board ships and spread from crew to crew. Tawhai hypothesizes that many of the songs originated instead in port-town taverns and were carried onto ships by sailors who learned them ashore.
Command of Evidence (Textual).prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Tawhai's hypothesis?
choices: The same songs were sung, with small variations, aboard ships from several different countries.
Tavern songbooks printed in port towns contain versions of many of the songs dated years earlier than any appearance of those songs in ships' logs or sailors' diaries.
Many of the songs describe the hardships of long voyages and the dangers of hunting whales.
Ships' logs frequently mention crews singing while hauling ropes or raising the anchor.
